equipment.note: Flammability map shows which material properties can burn in microgravity, guiding safer material selection for spacecraft.
Supports the Cone Calorimeter (Test 2) as a ground method to screen material fire hazard before flight.

profile.experiment_goal: The study set out to establish the burning conditions possible in a quiescent microgravity environment by using a gas burner to emulate real condensed fuels, in order to improve understanding of material flammability and assess existing flammability test methods for spacecraft fire safety.

glossary.definition: The near-weightless environment experienced in orbit, where flames behave very differently than on Earth.
The energy needed to turn a solid or liquid fuel into a gas so it can burn.
The energy released when a fuel burns completely.
A chart showing the conditions under which materials will burn.

key_facts.pressure: varied; nominal 14.7 psia (1 atm, 21% O2), 10.2 psia (0.7 atm, 26.5% O2), 8.2 psia (0.56 atm, 34% O2)
sensors: two heat flux transducers per burner
what_changed: fuel type (ethylene vs methane) and dilution

open_questions: Data analysis and publication of results were still underway, so the final report is expected to be updated.
The importance of flame radiation (represented by the laminar smoke point) in microgravity flames needs further study.
A clearer flammability plot adding oxygen mole fraction as a third dimension was still in progress.

results.result_expert: At 21% O2 and 14.7 psia, flames generally self-extinguished by radiative cooling, but at 27% O2/10.2 psia and 34% O2/8.2 psia they persisted for 3 minutes or more.
results.result_simple: Flames went out on their own in normal air (21% oxygen), but kept burning for 3 minutes or more in air with more oxygen and lower pressure.
results.safety_meaning: Shows which spacecraft air mixes let flames die out on their own, helping set safer oxygen and pressure levels for crew cabins.

results.result_expert: Emulation with heat of combustion ~24 kJ/g and heat of gasification ~3 kJ/g matched PMMA, a profound result showing a common plastic could burn steadily under NASA's proposed spacecraft atmospheres.
results.result_simple: The burner copied a common plastic (like PMMA) and showed it could burn steadily in the higher-oxygen, lower-pressure air NASA plans for future spacecraft.
results.safety_meaning: Warns that everyday plastics could keep burning in planned spacecraft air, so material choices matter for crew safety.

results.result_expert: The flammability map shows solid materials with heats of combustion 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity; the Cone Calorimeter (Test 2) can measure these properties.
results.result_simple: Solid materials with heats of combustion from 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in weightlessness.
results.safety_meaning: Defines the range of solid materials that can burn in weightlessness, guiding which materials are safe to use aboard spacecraft.

results.result_expert: Methane was hard to ignite compared with ethylene, and its flames tended to self-extinguish faster even at high oxygen concentration.
results.result_simple: Methane flames were harder to light than ethylene and went out faster, even when oxygen levels were high.
results.safety_meaning: Shows fuel type affects how easily a fire starts and lasts, useful for judging fire risk of different spacecraft fuel sources.

results.result_expert: Because the Cone Calorimeter (Test 2) can measure heat of combustion, heat of gasification, and surface re-radiation, the study suggests NASA may put more emphasis on Test 2 to assess material flammability.
results.result_simple: The results suggest NASA's Cone Calorimeter test (Test 2) could help predict whether materials will burn in spacecraft, so it may deserve more use.
results.safety_meaning: Points to a ground test that could screen spacecraft materials for fire hazard before flight, improving crew fire prevention.

profile.summary_expert: The Burning Rate Emulator used a flat porous gas burner (25 and 50 mm diameter) on the ISS to emulate quasi-steady burning of condensed fuels in quiescent microgravity. Tests used ethylene/nitrogen and methane/nitrogen mixtures across oxygen concentrations of 21% to 40% and pressures including 14.7 psia (21% O2), 10.2 psia (26.5% O2), and 8.2 psia (34% O2). The study mapped flammability in terms of heat of combustion, heat of gasification, and surface re-radiation. Flames generally self-extinguished at 21% O2 and 14.7 psia but persisted for 3 minutes or more at elevated oxygen and reduced pressure. Emulation with heat of combustion ~24 kJ/g and heat of gasification ~3 kJ/g matched PMMA, showing a common plastic could burn steadily under NASA's proposed spacecraft atmospheres. Solid materials with heats of combustion 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity.
profile.summary_simple: The study used a gas burner on the space station to copy how real solid and liquid fuels burn in weightlessness. Scientists wanted to learn which materials can keep burning in the air of a spacecraft. They found that common plastics can burn steadily in the higher-oxygen, lower-pressure air NASA is considering for future crewed missions.
